tier_reason: Tier raised from C to A. The simdjson paper (Langdale & Lemire, VLDB Journal 28(6) 2019, arXiv 1902.08318) is peer-reviewed; its Table 10 and Fig. 9 show sajson faster than RapidJSON 1.1.0 on all 14 files. The paper states the CPU (Intel i7-6700 Skylake), compiler (GCC 9.1) and flags (-O3 -march=native). The benchmark code is public in simdjson benchmark/parsingcompetition.cpp (tag v0.2.1), and the artifact repo simdjson/simdjson_experiments_vldb2019 runs it in experiments/comparison with a gcc:9.1 Docker image.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper text: "In practice, we find that another C++ parser, sajson, is faster [than RapidJSON]". Paper Table 10 (Skylake i7-6700, GCC 9.1, GB/s): sajson (static allocation) 0.62-1.2 vs RapidJSON insitu 0.41-1.0 and RapidJSON default 0.38-0.86. Examples: twitter 1.0 vs 0.72 insitu / 0.45 default; apache_builds 1.2 vs 0.80 / 0.48; canada 0.76 vs 0.43 / 0.43. Derived from page data: sajson is 1.10-1.77x faster than RapidJSON insitu (geomean ~1.4x) and 1.37-2.5x faster than RapidJSON default (geomean ~1.9x). Paper Table 9 (twitter, parse only): 1.0 vs 0.8 GB/s on Skylake and 0.9 vs 0.7 GB/s on Cannon Lake. README: "sajson's performance is excellent - it frequently benchmarks faster than RapidJSON, for example".
corrections.workload: Full in-memory parse with UTF-8 validation, single-threaded, best time. 14 files: apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc-2018, instruments, marine_ik, mesh, mesh.pretty, numbers, random, twitter, twitterescaped, update-center. sajson uses static (bounded) allocation. RapidJSON 1.1.0 runs with kParseValidateEncodingFlag in both default and insitu modes.
corrections.hardware: Paper: Intel i7-6700 Skylake, 3.4 GHz base / 3.7 GHz max, hyper-threading disabled; also Intel i3-8121U Cannon Lake. Author blog chart titles: Haswell i7-4771 (Windows 7, MSVC 14 and MinGW), Broadwell i5-5200U (Ubuntu 16.04, gcc/clang), iPhone SE (Xcode 8.3.2), Atom D2700 (Ubuntu, 64-bit).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper: GCC 9.1, -O3 -march=native, Linux, no PGO. Author blog harness (chadaustin/Web-Benchmarks json/SConstruct): -O2 -g -fno-exceptions -DNDEBUG -std=c++11 with gcc/clang (versions not stated); MSVC 14; Xcode 8.3.2.
corrections.caveats: Paper numbers use sajson's static-allocation mode. In dynamic-allocation mode (0.46-1.0 GB/s) sajson is slower than RapidJSON insitu on 6 of 14 files: citm_catalog, gsoc-2018, instruments, mesh.pretty, random and update-center. Snapshots are from 2018-2019: sajson 2018-09-20 and RapidJSON 1.1.0. sajson supports only 32-bit integers, does partial UTF-8 validation (it accepts some invalid sequences) and parses in situ (it modifies the input). The author's own 2017 blog numbers are only in chart images. That blog says that with GCC, RapidJSON, sajson and pjson are 'very similar'; its large wins (about 2-3x) are with MSVC, clang and iPhone builds. The repo's own benchmark/benchmark.cpp times only sajson and does not run RapidJSON.

notes: The original benchmark_url (the README #performance section) has only the verbatim qualitative sentence and no numbers. The numbers come from the author's 2017 blog charts (read from chart images) and from the independent peer-reviewed simdjson paper, which is now the benchmark_url. tier_reason: Tier raised from D to A on methodology. The independent, peer-reviewed simdjson paper (VLDB Journal 2019, arXiv 1902.08318) benchmarks jsmn against RapidJSON 1.1.0 and nlohmann/json ('JSON for Modern C++') on 14 files in its Table 10. It states the CPU (Intel i7-6700), compiler (GCC 9.1) and flags (-O3 -march=native). The code is public: simdjson benchmark/parsingcompetition.cpp built as allparsingcompetition with -DALLPARSER (tag v0.2.1), plus the artifact repo simdjson/simdjson_experiments_vldb2019. The win is only against nlohmann/json and only on 8 of 14 files.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The project claim "world fastest JSON parser/tokenizer" is not supported. Paper Table 10 (Skylake i7-6700, GCC 9.1, GB/s): jsmn beats JSON for Modern C++ (nlohmann/json) on 8 of 14 files, e.g. numbers 0.65 vs 0.06, github_events 0.52 vs 0.09, twitter 0.27 vs 0.10, instruments 0.24 vs 0.10. It is slower on the other 6: canada 0.01 vs 0.05, random 0.03 vs 0.07, apache_builds 0.07 vs 0.10, mesh 0.05 vs 0.06, mesh.pretty 0.09 vs 0.11, update-center 0.06 vs 0.07. Derived from page data: geomean ~1.5x faster than nlohmann/json. Against RapidJSON (default 0.38-0.86, insitu 0.41-1.0 GB/s), jsmn is slower on 12 of 14 files. It is faster only on numbers (0.65 vs 0.45) and on github_events against the default mode (0.52 vs 0.46).
corrections.workload: Tokenizing 14 in-memory JSON files (twitter, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc-2018, numbers, etc.), single-threaded, best time. jsmn_parse writes into a token array sized to the input, in the default build without JSMN_PARENT_LINKS. RapidJSON and nlohmann/json do full DOM parses.
corrections.hardware: Intel i7-6700 Skylake, 3.4 GHz, hyper-threading disabled (simdjson VLDB paper)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.1, -O3 -march=native, Linux (simdjson VLDB paper; simdjson v0.2.1 Makefile)
corrections.caveats: jsmn is only a tokenizer. It does not convert numbers, unescape strings, validate UTF-8 or build a queryable DOM, so a comparison with DOM parsers is not like-for-like. The paper says jsmn accepts invalid JSON such as [0e+]. The paper ran the default build without JSMN_PARENT_LINKS; the author's page says that build is 'terribly slow' on large objects (canada 0.01 GB/s). In the paper jsmn is slower than RapidJSON, sajson, gason and cJSON on most files. A 2012 third-party benchmark by Lev Walkin (lionet.livejournal.com/118853.html, code vlm/vlm-json-test) reports jsmn at 16 MB/s by default and 482 MB/s with the parent-links hack, vs yajl 249 MB/s, json-c 38 MB/s and Jansson 25 MB/s; it states no hardware or compiler. The README itself has no numbers. Last commit 2021-10-14.

notes: Kept because it is notable (4,194 stars). The tier rises to A because the methodology is complete, but the 'world fastest' claim is refuted and RapidJSON is not beaten. The only in-list baseline that loses is nlohmann/json, on 8 of 14 files. The orchestrator may want to flag this entry as a weak or mixed win. Metadata checks OK: MIT, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2021-10-14, abandoned.

tier_reason: Evidence is first-party only. The README chart (doc/benchmarks.png) and its raw timings in scripts/benchmark_plot.py come from the public benchmark sandbox/performance.cpp, which compares ser20, cereal and boost::serialization binary archives. No compiler, flags or CPU is stated, and there is no independent suite.

corrections.workload: Binary archive save to std::ostringstream and load from std::istringstream, 100-run averages, in sandbox/performance.cpp. That file is built by sandbox/CMakeLists.txt when Boost is found, not by doc/CMakeLists.txt. Data sets: vector<double> (1 to 1M), vector<uint8_t> (64M), vector<PoDStruct> (1 to 2M), vector<PoDChild> with a virtual base (1024, 32K), strings (200K to 20M chars), vector<string> (512 to 128K) and map<string,PoDStruct> (1024, 64K). The chart shows 6 categories, and the sizes behind each bar are not documented.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: "Ser20 is sometimes two times as fast as cereal and boost::serialization in binary serialization". Raw values in scripts/benchmark_plot.py (lower is faster), shown as ser20 vs cereal vs boost. PoDStruct: save 37.79 vs 75.25 vs 102.78, load 32.00 vs 58.57 vs 82.66. Map(PoDStruct): save 2.14 vs 4.48 vs 5.93, load 3.51 vs 4.58 vs 9.46. String: save 1.36 vs 2.51 vs 2.10, load 3.09 vs 4.07 vs 3.42. Derived from page data: about 1.3-2.1x faster than cereal and 1.1-2.8x faster than boost in these three categories. vector<double> and vector<uint8_t> are at parity. PoDChild load is slightly slower than cereal (26.27 vs 24.64).
corrections.caveats: The chart plots time normalized to cereal; lower is faster. Its raw values are in scripts/benchmark_plot.py. That dict has two "String" keys, so the second entry (probably the Vector(String) test) overwrites the first (a parity entry). No compiler, flags, CPU, or Boost/cereal versions are stated. The gain is attributed to buffering small ostream reads and writes. The README claims about '15% smaller' and 'compile up to 25% faster' have no data. GitHub does not mark the repo as a fork (fork:false), but the README calls it a C++20 fork of cereal. It is a small single-maintainer project (34 stars, 5 forks).

notes: The claim and the chart are accurate. The workload path was wrong: the benchmark is sandbox/performance.cpp, not something built by doc/CMakeLists.txt. The chart is labeled 'Relative performance: load/save' and its raw numbers are in the repo, so the record's 'unlabeled chart' caveat is fixed.
